topic: What happens if a rip current drags you out to sea?
title: Caught In A Rip Current
idea: A rip current pulls you out, not under; fighting it is what wears swimmers out, so float, swim sideways, wave.
hook: The sea is pulling you out. What's your first move?

beats.line: The beach shrinks, even though you're swimming hard toward it.
beats.see: Hero crawls hard toward shore but the paper beach slides away behind him like a treadmill; beach umbrellas shrink on 'shrinks'.

beats.line: A rip current flows out at up to eight feet per second.
beats.see: Top view: a narrow dark channel through the waves, arrows racing seaward; speed tag '8 FT/SEC' stamps on 'eight'.

beats.line: That's faster than an Olympic swimmer.
beats.see: A cutout Olympic swimmer with a gold medal races the arrow and falls behind on 'faster'.

beats.line: Fighting it wears out even strong swimmers. That's how people drown.
beats.see: Energy bar above the hero drains to red on 'wears', his arms slow; the bar blinks empty on 'drown'.

beats.line: Here's the twist. It pulls you out, not under.
beats.see: Side view underwater: the hero stays at the surface while the current slides him sideways out to sea; stamp OUT NOT UNDER on 'under'.

beats.line: One. Float. Let it carry you and save your energy.
beats.see: Step card 1 FLOAT; hero rolls onto his back on 'Float', energy bar stops draining on 'save'.

beats.line: Two. Swim sideways, along the beach, until it lets go.
beats.see: Step card 2 SWIM SIDEWAYS; hero swims parallel to shore, exits the dark channel on 'lets go' and the water calms.

beats.line: Three. Still stuck? Float and wave so a lifeguard sees you.
beats.see: Step card 3 WAVE; hero floats and waves one arm on 'wave', a lifeguard tower whistle blows on 'sees'.

end.line: Still swimming straight back? Float first, then save this.
end.see: Hero starts swimming at the shore again, freezes on 'Still'; the three step cards stack into one SAVE THIS card on 'save'.

description: A rip current is dragging you out to sea. Your first move decides everything. Save these three.

facts.claim: A rip current is a strong, narrow flow of water away from shore; it carries you out, it does not pull you under.
Rips can flow up to 8 feet per second, faster than an Olympic swimmer (typical 1 to 2 ft/s).
Swimming straight back against a rip exhausts even strong swimmers; rips are linked to an estimated 100+ US drownings a year.
Stay calm, don't fight it, float to save energy, swim parallel to shore until out of it; if you can't, float and wave or yell for help.
facts.source: NWS https://www.weather.gov/safety/beach-ripcurrents-hazards ; MacMahan / McCarroll 2014 on float-first order

notes: Big number '8 FT/SEC' is the maximum measured; line says 'up to'. 'That's how people drown' is an inference from NWS (exhaustion) plus the drowning estimate; if too strong, swap for 'That's what drowns swimmers.' or drop. No 'flip, float, follow' attribution. Step order float first, then sideways, per FACTS research note.
